7 Decisions

This chapter sets out the mathematical model of a decision (choices, states, outcomes, and utilities), represents decisions with matrices, and shows how ordinal utilities can be read off an agent’s preferences when those preferences form a weak order. It then turns to choice under ignorance, where we cannot assign probabilities to the states, and compares three norms: dominance, maximin (with its refinement, leximin), and minimax regret.

In Part I we learned about propositional logic and how it helps us analyze arguments and determine their tautological validity. In Part II we learned about probability, and how it helps us analyze probabilistic arguments. In this part, we’ll apply everything we learned in the previous two, plus some new techniques, to analyze how to make rational decisions. We start by considering those decisions that involve only one agent as a decision-maker, and then we move on to interactive decision theory—also known as game theory.

We start by setting out the main elements in our mathematical model of decisions. They are: choices, states, outcomes, and utilities. Choices are the options that the agent has: go to college, work on the family farm, or form a rock band, for instance. States are ways the world can be that affect what outcome your choice will have: whether the economy will tank in the next five years or not, for example. Outcomes are, precisely, a function of your choice on the one hand and the state of the world on the other: for instance, if you decide to work on the family farm and the economy tanks, the outcome is not as good as if it did not. Finally, utilities are a measure of your preferences over outcomes.

7.1 Representing decisions

The standard way of representing decisions is by using a matrix. For a decision with nnn choices and mmm states, we use an nnn by mmm matrix where the choices label the rows, the states label the columns and, the cells represent outcomes:

In general, we will write the utilities associated with the outcomes in each cell instead:

Suppose that we have a choice between going to the park or going to the movies. Those are our choices. It could rain or not. Those are the states. Pairing a choice with a state gives us an outcome, and so there are four of them: going to the park while it rains, going to the park while it doesn’t rain, going to the movies while it rains, and going to the movies while it doesn’t rain. Let us assume that your utilities for those four outcomes are 1, 4, 3, and 2 respectively (we will study where those utilities come from later in this chapter). A rained-out afternoon at the park is the worst thing that could happen to you, and a sunny one is the best; the movies are somewhere in the middle either way, and marginally better when it rains, since then at least you are not squandering good weather indoors. Writing PPP for going to the park, MMM for going to the movies, and RRR for its raining, we can represent this decision problem with the following matrix:

Not just any list of propositions will do for the columns of such a matrix. Suppose we had taken our states to be it rains and it snows. Then a clear day is a way things might turn out that no column covers, and the matrix simply says nothing about what would happen if it came about—our list of outcomes would be incomplete. Suppose instead that we had taken our states to be it rains and it is cold. Now a cold, rainy day falls under both columns at once, and the cells disagree with each other about what its outcome is. To rule out both defects, we require that the states partition the possibility space:

Definition 7.1. Partition: A set of propositions {S1,S2,…,Sn}\{S_{1}, S_{2}, \ldots, S_{n}\}{S1​,S2​,…,Sn​} is a partition of the possibility space if and only if exactly one of them is true in each possible world. That is to say, they must be both:

  1. Mutually exclusive: no two of them are true in the same possible world (see Definition 4.1); and

  2. Jointly exhaustive: there is no possible world in which none of them is true.

Mutual exclusivity is what rules out the second bad case, and joint exhaustiveness what rules out the first. Together they guarantee that, however things turn out, exactly one column describes the situation you are actually in—which is what entitles us to read each row as a complete specification of what a choice would get you.

Our original example passes the test, and does so for a reason that will often be useful: a proposition and its negation always form a partition, since as a matter of logic RRR and ¬R\neg R¬R cannot both be true and cannot both be false. The rows of a truth-table are a partition as well: exactly one row describes any given possible world, which is precisely why the probabilities we assign to the rows of a stochastic truth-table have to sum to 1.

7.2 Where do ordinal utilities come from?

Where did the utility numbers come from? The answer is: from your preferences among outcomes. Utilities are a scale we use to represent your preferences. We will consider two different kinds of utility scales, ordinal and cardinal. We start with ordinal scales in this chapter, and turn to cardinal scales in Chapter 8.

We will use the symbol "≻\succ≻" to represent preference relations—φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ means that the agent prefers φ\varphiφ to ψ\psiψ. If an agent is indifferent between φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, we will write φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ. Recall that your most preferred option is a sunny day at the park, which you prefer even to the movies when it rains; that you prefer being at the movies when it rains to being at the movies when it doesn’t; and that you prefer being at the movies when it doesn’t rain even to being at the park when it rains. We can therefore represent these preferences as follows:

(P∧¬R)≻(M∧R)(P \land \neg R) \succ (M \land R)(P∧¬R)≻(M∧R)
(M∧R)≻(M∧¬R)(M \land R) \succ (M \land \neg R)(M∧R)≻(M∧¬R)
(M∧¬R)≻(P∧R)(M \land \neg R) \succ (P \land R)(M∧¬R)≻(P∧R)

Notice that we have not stated all of your preferences here, because we have not stated that you prefer being at the park when it doesn’t rain to being at the movies when it doesn’t rain. You might think that goes without saying, given that you prefer being at the park when it doesn’t rain to being at the movies when it rains, and you prefer being at the movies when it rains to being at the movies when it doesn’t rain. That is to say, you might think it goes without saying that your preferences should be transitive. If so, decision theorists agree with you. In fact, decision theory presupposes that your preferences satisfy several global constraints:

Definition 7.2. Asymmetric: An agent’s preferences are asymmetric if and only if, for any two outcomes φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ:

  1. If φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ, then not ψ≻φ\psi \succ \varphiψ≻φ.

  2. If φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ, then not ψ∼φ\psi \sim \varphiψ∼φ.

  3. If φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ, then not φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ and also not ψ≻φ\psi \succ \varphiψ≻φ.

Definition 7.3. Transitive: An agent’s preferences are transitive if and only if, for any three outcomes χ\chiχ, φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ:

  1. If φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ and ψ≻χ\psi \succ \chiψ≻χ, then φ≻χ\varphi \succ \chiφ≻χ.

  2. If φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ and ψ∼χ\psi \sim \chiψ∼χ, then φ∼χ\varphi \sim \chiφ∼χ.

  3. If φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ and ψ∼χ\psi \sim \chiψ∼χ, then φ≻χ\varphi \succ \chiφ≻χ.

  4. If φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ and ψ≻χ\psi \succ \chiψ≻χ, then φ≻χ\varphi \succ \chiφ≻χ.

Definition 7.4. Connected: An agent’s preferences are connected if and only if, for any two outcomes φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ, at least one of the following holds:

  1. φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ.

  2. ψ≻φ\psi \succ \varphiψ≻φ.

  3. φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ.

Notice that Definition 7.2 and Definition 7.4 work together: connectedness guarantees that at least one of the three relations holds between any two outcomes, and asymmetry guarantees that at most one of them does. Taken together, then, they tell us that for any two outcomes exactly one of φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ, ψ≻φ\psi \succ \varphiψ≻φ, and φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ is true—an agent whose preferences satisfy both is never undecided between two outcomes, and never prefers each of two outcomes to the other.

Notice also the crucial distinction between being indifferent between two outcomes, on the one hand, and having no preference relations whatsoever between them, not even indifference. If you are indifferent between two outcomes, that means that you are completely willing to replace one with the other. Right now, for instance, I am indifferent between having coffee and tea—I could go for either one. On the other hand, some people have no preference relations between The Rolling Stones and Mozart. It’s not that they are indifferent between them—it’s rather that they think that they each have different properties that make them incommensurable—they just cannot compare one to the other. For better or worse, Definition 7.4 prohibits these incommensurable outcomes. Normal humans also sometimes have intransitive preferences. Suppose you add a single grain of sugar to successive cups of coffee. Normal humans will be indifferent between neighboring cups of coffee, but will definitely have a preference between the first and the last.

What does the fact that we violate some of these conditions mean for the theory of decision that presupposes that we don’t? We won’t deal with this issue here at all, except to make the following two points: first, decision theory is at least partly normative—it tells us not how our preferences actually are ordered, but how they should be ordered if we are to make rational decisions; second, there is some comfort in the fact that we can make rational decisions even when we don’t satisfy all the structural conditions on preferences—for instance, even if your preferences are not connected among all the possible choices for dessert, but you know you can have your first choice, the lack of connectedness doesn’t matter for that particular choice.

If an agent’s preferences do satisfy all the structural conditions on preferences, we will say that his preferences form a weak order:

Definition 7.5. Weak order: An agent’s preferences form a weak order if and only if they are connected, asymmetric, and transitive.

If your preferences form a weak order, then they can be represented by a ranking. The agent’s preferences in movies/park case, for example, can be represented in the following ranking (ordered from best to worst top to bottom):

  • P∧¬RP \land \neg RP∧¬R

  • M∧RM \land RM∧R

  • M∧¬RM \land \neg RM∧¬R

  • P∧RP \land RP∧R

Of course, the structural definitions allow ties, but in this case the agent is not indifferent between any of the outcomes.

Once we have a ranking (with ties allowed), we can assign a number to each outcome reflecting its place in the ranking, with higher numbers assigned to higher-ranked outcomes. For instance, we could have the following numbers assigned to the outcomes for the movies/park case:

  1. P∧¬RP \land \neg RP∧¬R
  2. M∧RM \land RM∧R
  3. M∧¬RM \land \neg RM∧¬R
  4. P∧RP \land RP∧R

Other than assigning higher numbers to higher-ranked outcomes, we are free to assign whatever number we wish. For instance, this other assignment is just as good as the previous one:

  • 2000 P∧¬RP \land \neg RP∧¬R
  • 1395 M∧RM \land RM∧R
  • 2 M∧¬RM \land \neg RM∧¬R
  • -12 P∧RP \land RP∧R

We call the number assigned to an outcome its utility, and we write it u(Oi)=nu(O_{i}) = nu(Oi​)=n. If the utility function uuu satisfies the requirement just laid out, we say that it is an ordinal utility function:

Definition 7.6. Ordinal utility function: A utility function uuu is ordinal if and only if, for any two outcomes φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ:

  • a u(φ)>u(ψ)u(\varphi) > u (\psi)u(φ)>u(ψ) if and only if φ≻ψ\varphi \succ \psiφ≻ψ; and
  • b u(φ)=u(ψ)u(\varphi) = u(\psi)u(φ)=u(ψ) if and only if φ∼ψ\varphi \sim \psiφ∼ψ.

The numbers in an ordinal utility function represent nothing more and nothing less than the order of the corresponding outcome in the ranking of the agent’s preferences. If uuu is a correct ordinal representation of an agent’s preferences, then any ordinal transformation u′u'u′ of uuu will also be a correct ordinal representation of those preferences:

Definition 7.7. Ordinal transformation: u′u'u′ is an ordinal transformation of uuu if and only if, for every two outcomes φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ: u′(φ)≥u′(ψ)u'(\varphi) \geq u'(\psi)u′(φ)≥u′(ψ) if and only if u(φ)≥u(ψ)u(\varphi) \geq u(\psi)u(φ)≥u(ψ)

7.3 Choice under ignorance

Decision theorists usually distinguish between three different kinds of decisions: decisions under certainty, decisions under ignorance, and decisions under risk. A decision counts as a decision under certainty when the agent is certain which state in the partition obtains. Decision under certainty need not be computationally easy (the mathematical theory of linear programming has been fruitfully applied to this topic), but theoretically does not give rise to very interesting topics, and therefore we shall not dwell on it any more.

When agents cannot eliminate all but one of the states in the relevant partition, but can assign probabilities to those states, we are dealing with decisions under risk. We will deal with those kinds of decisions in the next chapter. Finally, when subjects cannot even assign meaningful probabilities to the states of the relevant partition, we are dealing with decisions under ignorance. That is what we will be dealing with in the rest of this chapter.

7.3.1 Dominance

Suppose that, in the movies/park example, we have no idea whether it will rain or not. Having no idea is very different from being 50/50 on whether it will rain or not—the latter would be a decision under risk, whereas if we genuinely have no idea then we are facing a decision under ignorance. You might think that there is not much that can be said about how to go about making decisions when we are completely ignorant regarding the probabilities of the different possible states, but you’d be wrong. Consider, for instance, a slight variation of our movies/park example, one where your ranking (together with a possible ordinal utility function) is instead as follows:

  1. P∧¬RP \land \neg RP∧¬R
  2. P∧RP \land RP∧R
  3. M∧¬RM \land \neg RM∧¬R
  4. M∧RM \land RM∧R

The matrix corresponding to that ranking is then the following:

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through dominance on this matrix.

Something remarkable about this ranking of outcomes is that, no matter whether it rains or not, you prefer to go to the park than to go to the movies. So, even if you are completely ignorant of whether it is going to rain or not, you should go to the park: you will then get your preferred outcome no matter what state the world is in.

When that happens—i.e., when one choice results in a better outcome than all the other ones no matter what state obtains—we say that the choice in question dominates the other. We will define both a strong and a weak form of dominance:

Definition 7.8. Strong dominance: Option φ\varphiφ strongly dominates option ψ\psiψ if and only if, for every state SiS_{i}Si​, u(φ∧Si)>u(ψ∧Si).u(\varphi \land S_{i}) > u(\psi \land S_{i}).u(φ∧Si​)>u(ψ∧Si​).

Definition 7.9. Weak dominance: Option φ\varphiφ weakly dominates option ψ\psiψ if and only if, for every state SiS_{i}Si​, u(φ∧Si)≥u(ψ∧Si),u(\varphi \land S_{i}) \geq u(\psi \land S_{i}),u(φ∧Si​)≥u(ψ∧Si​), and for at least one state SjS_{j}Sj​, u(φ∧Sj)>u(ψ∧Sj).u(\varphi \land S_{j}) > u(\psi \land S_{j}).u(φ∧Sj​)>u(ψ∧Sj​).

And, on the basis of those definitions, we will propose our first norm for decisions:

Norm 7.10. Dominance norm: dominated options are irrational

Notice that the dominance norm doesn’t tell us which option is rational, it only tells us which are irrational—namely, the dominated ones. In the special case where there are only two options, if one of them is dominated then the Dominance norm entails that the other one is the only rationally permissible one. But for cases with more than two options, the fact that one is dominated does not immediately tell you which option is rationally required.

If for two given choices neither one of them is dominated by the other, there are still two other possibilities: it may be that they have the same utility for every state (in which case we’ll say that they are equivalent), or it may be that one of them has a higher utility for at least one state, and the other one has a higher utility for at least one other state (in which case we’ll say that they are crossing):

Definition 7.11. Equivalent: Options φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are equivalent if and only if, for every state SiS_{i}Si​, u(φ∧Si)=u(ψ∧Si).u(\varphi \land S_{i}) = u(\psi \land S_{i}).u(φ∧Si​)=u(ψ∧Si​).

Definition 7.12. Crossing: Options φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are crossing if and only if there is some state SiS_{i}Si​ such that u(φ∧Si)>u(ψ∧Si),u(\varphi \land S_{i}) > u(\psi \land S_{i}),u(φ∧Si​)>u(ψ∧Si​), and some state SjS_{j}Sj​ such that u(ψ∧Sj)>u(φ∧Sj).u(\psi \land S_{j}) > u(\varphi \land S_{j}).u(ψ∧Sj​)>u(φ∧Sj​).

7.3.2 Maximin

Whereas the dominance rule only tells us which choices are irrational, there are other rules for decision under ignorance which tell us which choices are rational. One of them, the maximin norm, tells us to maximize the minimum utility. To do this, we have to first figure out, for each choice, what is the minimum utility it can give us. Then we see which choice has the maximum of these minima. Of course, there may be ties. In that case, we can once again apply the maximin norm to the remaining utilities (eliminating first the minima from the previous steps). If we write min⁡iu(φ∧Si)\min_{i} u(\varphi \land S_{i})mini​u(φ∧Si​) for the minimum utility that option φ\varphiφ yields across all states SiS_{i}Si​—that is, φ\varphiφ’s worst-case utility—then the two norms are the following:

Norm 7.13. Maximin norm: Option φ\varphiφ is (maximin-)rational if and only if min⁡iu(φ∧Si)≥min⁡iu(ψ∧Si)\min_{i} u(\varphi \land S_{i}) \geq \min_{i} u(\psi \land S_{i})imin​u(φ∧Si​)≥imin​u(ψ∧Si​) for every other option ψ\psiψ.

Norm 7.14. Leximin norm: Let u(1)(φ)≤u(2)(φ)≤⋯≤u(n)(φ)u_{(1)}(\varphi) \leq u_{(2)}(\varphi) \leq \dots \leq u_{(n)}(\varphi)u(1)​(φ)≤u(2)​(φ)≤⋯≤u(n)​(φ) be the utilities of φ\varphiφ across all states, arranged from lowest to highest. Option φ\varphiφ is leximin-rational if and only if, for every other option ψ\psiψ, either u(k)(φ)=u(k)(ψ) for every k,u_{(k)}(\varphi) = u_{(k)}(\psi) \text{ for every } k,u(k)​(φ)=u(k)​(ψ) for every k, or there is some kkk such that u(k)(φ)>u(k)(ψ)u_{(k)}(\varphi) > u_{(k)}(\psi)u(k)​(φ)>u(k)​(ψ) and u(j)(φ)=u(j)(ψ)u_{(j)}(\varphi) = u_{(j)}(\psi)u(j)​(φ)=u(j)​(ψ) for every j<kj < kj<k.

Going through Table 7.8 choice by choice, the minimum utility of A1A_1A1​ is 000, the minimum utility of A2A_2A2​ is −1-1−1, the minimum utility of A3A_3A3​ is 111, and the minimum utility of A4A_4A4​ is 333. Of those four minima, 333 is the largest, and it belongs to A4A_4A4​ alone: no other option has a worst case that good. So, by Norm 7.13, A4A_4A4​ is the uniquely maximin-rational choice.

Sometimes, though, maximin does not settle on a unique choice, because two or more choices are tied for the best worst case. When that happens, we turn to leximin, which, as we saw, tries to break the tie by looking at the second-worst utility of each of the tied choices (and, if they are tied there too, the third-worst, and so on). But even leximin can fail to settle on a unique choice, as the following decision problem, involving four choices and five states, illustrates.

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through maximin and leximin on this matrix.

In Table 7.9, every choice has the same minimum utility, 000, so maximin alone cannot distinguish between them. To apply leximin, we arrange each choice’s utilities from lowest to highest: A1A_1A1​’s become (0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5), A2A_2A2​’s become (0,1,1,2,3)(0,1,1,2,3)(0,1,1,2,3), A3A_3A3​’s become (0,1,2,3,3)(0,1,2,3,3)(0,1,2,3,3), and A4A_4A4​’s become (0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5). Comparing these term by term, all four choices agree on the lowest utility (000) and on the second-lowest (111), so the tie is not yet broken. At the third-lowest utility, however, A2A_2A2​ (with 111) and A3A_3A3​ (with 222) both fall below A1A_1A1​ and A4A_4A4​ (which each have 333 there), so by Norm 7.14 both A2A_2A2​ and A3A_3A3​ are eliminated. That leaves A1A_1A1​ and A4A_4A4​, and, as it turns out, their utilities sorted from lowest to highest are exactly the same: (0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5)(0,1,3,4,5) in both cases. So leximin narrows the field down to A1A_1A1​ and A4A_4A4​, but—since their sorted utilities agree at every position—it cannot tell us which of the two to choose.

7.3.3 Minimax regret

Consider what happens when we try to apply maximin to the following table:

Strictly speaking, we cannot apply any decision rule to Table 7.10 because it has amounts of money instead of utilities in the cells. But for anyone whose preferences over money is more or less normal, the corresponding utilities will have the result that the maximin norm tells us to go with A1A_{1}A1​ because it has the maximum minimal utility possible (50 cents more than A2A_{2}A2​). That is to say, the maximin rule is telling us to forgo an opportunity to gain $10,000 in order to save $0.50. Many would find that ridiculous. Those who do think that the regret you would feel if S2S_{2}S2​ obtains and you miss out on $10,000 is much greater than the relief you would feel if S1S_{1}S1​ obtains and you gain $0.5.

Let us formalize this view a bit. Let us define MAXi\mathrm{MAX}_{i}MAXi​ to be the highest utility that any of the available options yields in state SiS_{i}Si​—i.e., the largest number in that state’s column: MAXi=max⁡φu(φ∧Si)\mathrm{MAX}_{i} = \max_{\varphi} u(\varphi \land S_{i})MAXi​=maxφ​u(φ∧Si​). Then the regret associated with u(φ∧Si)u(\varphi \land S_{i})u(φ∧Si​) is the result of subtracting that value from the maximum for that state: r(φ∧Si)=MAXi−u(φ∧Si)r(\varphi \land S_{i}) = \mathrm{MAX}_{i} - u(\varphi \land S_{i})r(φ∧Si​)=MAXi​−u(φ∧Si​).

This suggests a new norm: instead of maximizing the minimum utility, minimize the maximum regret.

Norm 7.15. Minimax regret norm: Option φ\varphiφ is minimax-regret-rational if and only if max⁡ir(φ∧Si)≤max⁡ir(ψ∧Si)\max_{i} r(\varphi \land S_{i}) \leq \max_{i} r(\psi \land S_{i})imax​r(φ∧Si​)≤imax​r(ψ∧Si​) for every other option ψ\psiψ.

Returning to Table 7.10: MAX1=$1.50\mathrm{MAX}_{1} = \$1.50MAX1​=$1.50 and MAX2=$10,000\mathrm{MAX}_{2} = \$10{,}000MAX2​=$10,000. So A1A_1A1​’s regret is $0 in S1S_1S1​ (since it achieves the maximum there) and $9,998.25 in S2S_2S2​, for a maximum regret of $9,998.25; while A2A_2A2​’s regret is $0.50 in S1S_1S1​ and $0 in S2S_2S2​, for a maximum regret of only $0.50. By Norm 7.15, then, minimax regret recommends A2A_2A2​—the reverse of what maximin recommended, and, to many people, the more sensible verdict.

To see how a regret table is built from a utility table, and how minimax regret is applied to it, consider the following decision problem, involving four choices and three states.

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through minimax regret on this matrix.

We build the regret table one state at a time. In S1S_1S1​, the highest utility anyone achieves is 666 (by A3A_3A3​), so MAX1=6\mathrm{MAX}_{1} = 6MAX1​=6; in S2S_2S2​, the highest is 555 (by A2A_2A2​), so MAX2=5\mathrm{MAX}_{2} = 5MAX2​=5; and in S3S_3S3​, the highest is 666 (by A1A_1A1​), so MAX3=6\mathrm{MAX}_{3} = 6MAX3​=6. Subtracting each choice’s utility from the relevant MAXi\mathrm{MAX}_iMAXi​ gives us the regret table below, where we star each choice’s maximum regret and double-star the choice whose maximum regret is itself the minimum among all the maxima.

Going through Table 7.12 choice by choice, the maximum regret of A1A_1A1​ is 444, the maximum regret of A2A_2A2​ is 444, the maximum regret of A3A_3A3​ is 555, and the maximum regret of A4A_4A4​ is 333. Of those four maxima, 333 is the smallest, and it belongs to A4A_4A4​ alone. So, by Norm 7.15, A4A_4A4​ is the uniquely minimax-regret-rational choice.

Now, maximin (and leximin) have a notable virtue that minimax regret lacks: they only need to know how the outcomes are ranked, not by how much one outcome is better than another. If we transform every utility in a decision problem by any function that preserves the original ranking of the outcomes—an ordinal transformation—maximin and leximin will always recommend the very same choice, since they only ever compare utilities using >>>, ≥\geq≥, or ===, and no ordinal transformation can change the truth value of any of those comparisons. Minimax regret, however, essentially involves subtraction, and ordinal transformations do not, in general, preserve differences between numbers. So minimax regret’s recommendation can change under a transformation that leaves maximin’s recommendation exactly where it was.

To see this, consider what happens if we square every utility in Table 7.11—a legitimate ordinal transformation, since squaring is strictly increasing on positive numbers, and hence preserves the ranking of every outcome.

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through minimax regret on this matrix.

The minimum utility of A1A_1A1​ is now 111, of A2A_2A2​ is 444, of A3A_3A3​ is 111, and of A4A_4A4​ is 999—so, just as before, A4A_4A4​ has the largest minimum, and maximin still uniquely recommends A4A_4A4​. Minimax regret, however, tells a different story. Now MAX1=36\mathrm{MAX}_{1} = 36MAX1​=36, MAX2=25\mathrm{MAX}_{2} = 25MAX2​=25, and MAX3=36\mathrm{MAX}_{3} = 36MAX3​=36, which gives us the following regret table.

The maximum regrets are now 242424 for A1A_1A1​, 323232 for A2A_2A2​, 353535 for A3A_3A3​, and 272727 for A4A_4A4​—so minimax regret now uniquely recommends A1A_1A1​, the very choice it had previously ranked worst but one. Simply squaring the utilities—without changing how any outcome is ranked relative to any other—was enough to flip minimax regret’s recommendation from A4A_4A4​ to A1A_1A1​, even though maximin’s recommendation did not budge. This shows that minimax regret, unlike maximin and leximin, is not a purely ordinal norm: it presupposes that differences in utility are themselves meaningful, and can be compared to one another.

Minimax regret has a second, and arguably more troubling, defect: it can violate a principle we might call independence of irrelevant alternatives—roughly, the idea that whether φ\varphiφ or ψ\psiψ is recommended should not depend on which other choices happen to also be on the table, so long as neither of those other choices is itself the one recommended. To see minimax regret violate this principle, suppose our decision problem initially involves just two choices, AAA and BBB, and two states.

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through minimax regret on this matrix.

Here MAX1=10\mathrm{MAX}_{1} = 10MAX1​=10 and MAX2=10\mathrm{MAX}_{2} = 10MAX2​=10, so AAA’s regret is (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), for a maximum of 111, while BBB’s regret is (0,2)(0,2)(0,2), for a maximum of 222. By Norm 7.15, minimax regret recommends AAA. Now suppose a third choice, CCC, becomes available—one that does very well in S1S_1S1​ and very poorly in S2S_2S2​.

Try it in the Decisions Lab Step through minimax regret on this matrix.

Adding CCC raises MAX1\mathrm{MAX}_{1}MAX1​ from 101010 to 151515, which increases everyone’s regret in S1S_1S1​. AAA’s regret is now (6,0)(6,0)(6,0), for a maximum of 666; BBB’s regret is now (5,2)(5,2)(5,2), for a maximum of 555; and CCC’s own regret is (0,8)(0,8)(0,8), for a maximum of 888. Minimax regret now recommends BBB, not AAA—even though CCC, the newcomer, is not itself recommended, and nothing about AAA’s or BBB’s own prospects changed at all. It would not be strange if adding CCC to the menu sometimes changed the recommendation to CCC itself—that would just mean CCC turned out to be a good choice. What is strange is that merely adding CCC can flip the verdict between the two choices that were already on the table, even though CCC never had a chance of being recommended in the first place.

Finally, minimax regret can recommend choices that seem straightforwardly wrong. Consider a decision problem with a hundred states, and two choices: A1A_1A1​, which yields 100100100 in S1S_1S1​ and nothing at all in every other state, and A2A_2A2​, which yields nothing in S1S_1S1​ but 999999 in every one of the other ninety-nine states.

Intuitively, A2A_2A2​ looks like the obviously better choice: it guarantees a solidly good outcome in ninety-nine out of a hundred states, while A1A_1A1​ only pays off in a single state, and leaves us with nothing in all the rest. But minimax regret disagrees. MAX1=100\mathrm{MAX}_{1} = 100MAX1​=100 and MAXi=99\mathrm{MAX}_{i} = 99MAXi​=99 for every i>1i > 1i>1. So A1A_1A1​’s regret is 000 in S1S_1S1​ and 999999 in every other state, for a maximum regret of 999999; while A2A_2A2​’s regret is 100100100 in S1S_1S1​ and 000 everywhere else, for a maximum regret of 100100100. Since 99<10099 < 10099<100, minimax regret recommends A1A_1A1​—the choice that, intuitively, we should avoid.

There is, however, a standard reply to this last objection: given that we are dealing with a decision under ignorance, we have no idea about the relative probabilities of the 100 states. For all we know, S1S_{1}S1​ has a 99.9999% chance of obtaining, while the remaining 99 states have almost 0 chance each. If, on the other hand, we do have at least some idea of the probabilities of the states, then we are dealing with a decision under risk, which is the topic of our next chapter.

Exercises

  1. What happens to an ordinal scale when it is transformed by multiplying each number by -1? By 0? Are these acceptable transformations of the original scale? Why or why not?

    Show solution

    Multiplying by −1-1−1 reverses the order of the outcomes, and multiplying by 000 makes every outcome tie, so neither transformation preserves the ordinal ranking. Neither is acceptable.
